etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English saucer, from Old French saussier (and feminine saussiere; hence modern French saucier m, saucière f).

definitions.definition: A small shallow dish to hold a cup and catch drips.
An object round and gently curved, shaped like a saucer.
(obsolete) A small pan or other vessel-like food container in which sauce was set on a table.

quote.citation: 1627 (indicated as 1626), Francis [Bacon], “II. Century.”, in Sylua Syluarum: Or A Naturall Historie. In Ten Centuries. […], London:  […]  William Rawley […]; [p]rinted by J[ohn] H[aviland] for William Lee […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Take two saucers , and strike the edge of the one against the bottom of the other , within a pail of water ; and you shall find , that as you put the saucers lower and lower , the sound groweth more flat

definitions.definition: A flat, shallow caisson for raising sunken ships.
A shallow socket for the pivot of a capstan.
(transitive) To pour (tea, etc.) from the cup into the saucer in order to cool it before drinking.
(intransitive) Of the eyes: to become large and round.

quote.text: Lydia's eyes saucered with shock. Her heart was beating very fast and all her adrenaline kicked in.
